notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on Ruth 2 below. I hit the tool limit partway through, so some sources are missing. Two full commentaries got cut off: Gill stops after v. 14 and the Pulpit Commentary after v. 15. For vv. 15–23 I used the aggregate commentary pages and search results instead. I couldn't reach Ellicott, the NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey, or the Catholic and Orthodox commentary sites. I also found nothing from Methodist, Lutheran or Pentecostal teachers, or about prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out.

**Sources:**
- **EW** = Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-2/
- **Pulpit** = Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ruth/2.htm
- **Gill** = Gill's Exposition: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/2.htm

---

**v. 1**
- Boaz was related to Naomi through her dead husband Elimelech, but we aren't told exactly how. Boaz stayed in Bethlehem through the famine and prospered, which suggests the family's move to Moab didn't have to happen. The phrase "man of great wealth" is the one elsewhere translated "mighty man of valour," and Leon Morris compares it to our word "knight." EW
- Pulpit says the Hebrew can mean strength, valour, wealth or ability, and the writer seems to mean "a strong and substantial yeoman." The word for "relative" first means "acquaintance," though here it means kin. The meaning of the name Boaz is uncertain. Pulpit
- Gill reads the phrase as wealth, power and virtue together. The Targum adds that Boaz was "mighty in the law." Gill passes on Jewish claims that Boaz was the judge Ibzan, grandson of Nahshon, and son of Salmon and Rahab (citing Matt 1:5). He also wonders why Boaz hadn't already helped Naomi; perhaps he didn't know how poor she was. Gill

**v. 2**
- Gleaning was Israel's care for the poor under Lev 19:9–10. Owners had to be generous, and the poor still worked for their food, which kept their dignity. Ruth took the initiative herself, and she wasn't being "more spiritual" by staying home to pray for food. EW
- Gleaning was humbling for someone used to giving. Ruth asks Naomi's leave politely, and Naomi agrees. Field boundaries were open land marked by stones, not walls. Pulpit
- Ruth may not have known the gleaning law, or knew it but was too modest to use it without permission. Gill suggests Naomi's consent may have been prompted by the Spirit, since it led to Ruth becoming an ancestor of Christ. Gill

**v. 3**
- It looked like chance to Ruth, but God was guiding her. God's hand often works through ordinary actions and is usually seen only looking back. EW
- What seemed to Ruth like "hap" or luck was really God's purpose and providence. Gill
- Ruth's steps were "ordered." Pulpit also mentions later rabbinic rules on gleaning, such as one or two fallen stalks going to the poor but three going to the owner. Pulpit
- Piper: Ruth did not just happen to come to Boaz's field. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-under-the-wings-of-god

**v. 4**
- How Boaz greets his workers, and how they answer, shows his character as a master. EW
- Pulpit calls it courtesy meeting courtesy. Pulpit quotes Thomson that such greetings are still common in the East. Pulpit
- A rich man supervising his own field showed both effort and humility. The greetings were polite, but Gill sees real faith in them, a sense that nothing succeeds without God's blessing. The Targum reads "may the Word of the Lord be your help." Gill

**v. 5**
- Boaz asks "whose," not "who." Ruth didn't look like an ordinary pauper, so he wondered which family she belonged to. Pulpit dismisses as fanciful the rabbinic idea that Boaz admired her for leaving the bundles of three stalks. Pulpit
- Aben Ezra thought Boaz assumed she was someone's wife. The Targum asks "of what nation is she?" Gill

**v. 6**
- Pulpit prefers the indefinite "a Moabite young woman." Pulpit
- The Targum has the foreman add that she had become a proselyte (a convert). Gill

**v. 7**
- Ruth asked politely for what was legally hers. She didn't know she was being watched, and her hard work impressed Boaz. Guzik's application: others watch how we walk with God too. EW
- Pulpit suggests the clause may mean "gather into bundles," since gleaning "among the sheaves" was only granted later (v. 15). The "house" was a hut or shelter in the field, and Ruth's rest there was short. Pulpit
- Gill agrees it was a booth in the field, not Naomi's home. He rejects the Septuagint's "until evening." Gill

**v. 8**
- In Boaz's field Ruth would find company among the young women. Boaz shows kindness with no sign yet of romance or expected return. EW
- "My daughter" is fatherly, suggesting Boaz was older. Pulpit
- Gill also infers Boaz's age from "my daughter." Gill

**v. 9**
- Boaz offers protection ("not to touch you") and refreshment (water). EW
- The water may have come from the well by Bethlehem's gate that David later longed for (2 Sam 23:15). Gleaners didn't normally get free water, so this was a special privilege. Pulpit
- The order not to touch her meant no harm, rudeness or "wanton tricks." Gill

**v. 10**
- Ruth asks why this good thing has come, not why the hard things came. Her being a foreigner made the kindness more precious. Guzik applies it to welcoming outsiders. EW
- Ruth doesn't lament her lot. She thanks Boaz for the first thing he did, which was simply noticing her. The Hebrew puns on "notice me" (*hikkiréni*) and "foreigner" (*nokriyyah*). Pulpit
- The Targum glosses "foreigner" as one of the daughters of Moab, a people not allowed into the congregation. Gill

**v. 11**
- Small-town news travelled fast, and Ruth's loyalty to Naomi was noticed. EW
- Pulpit quotes Lawson that Ruth didn't praise herself, and links this to "he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." "Heretofore" is literally "yesterday and the day before." Pulpit
- A Midrash reads "left thy father and mother" figuratively, as leaving her idols. Gill

**v. 12**
- Boaz speaks to Ruth as to a new convert who trusts Israel's God, has left her old ties, and is humble. His words are also a prayer for her. Guzik quotes Spurgeon urging older Christians to encourage new converts. Morris sees the "wings" as a small bird under its mother's wings (Ps 17:8; 36:7). EW
- Fuller pictures a hen gathering her chicks. Pulpit
- The two clauses mean reward in this world and in the world to come (the Targum). Gill says the reward is "not of debt, but of grace" and Ruth's good works don't earn it. The wings may be a bird's or the cherubim's. "Under the wings" became a Jewish phrase for conversion, and the Targum reads "under the wings of the Shekinah." Gill
- Piper: Ruth has not *earned* mercy. Taking refuge under God's wings gave her the freedom to love Naomi. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-under-the-wings-of-god

**v. 13**
- Ruth's words are a polite thank-you. EW
- Pulpit reads it as a wish, "may I continue to find favour," and "my lord" as polite humility. Pulpit
- Gill instead reads it as confident: "I shall find favour." The Septuagint and Syriac drop the "not," giving "I shall be as one of thine handmaids." Gill

**v. 14**
- Guzik sees a first hint of romance. Ruth kept food back so as not to look greedy, and to take some home. He also reads it as a picture of outsiders who accept Christ's invitation and are satisfied, quoting Spurgeon. EW
- "At mealtime" belongs to the narrator, not to Boaz's words. The "vinegar" was a cooling sour wine. "Reached" may mean "made into a bunch" of roasted ears. Pulpit
- Ruth sat to one side of the reapers out of modesty. A Midrash reads the bread as the Messiah's kingdom and the vinegar as his sufferings (Isa 53:5). Gill

**v. 15**
- Letting her glean among the sheaves went beyond Lev 19. EW
- Boaz probably gave the order where Ruth could hear it. Pulpit

**v. 16**
- Boaz let grain fall "by accident" so she wouldn't feel like a charity case. EW
- Henry: masters should allow their servants to be charitable. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/2-16.html
- Henry's Concise Commentary sees in Boaz's kindness a picture of Christ's kindness to sinners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/2-16.htm
- Spurgeon makes the reapers ministers who must drop "handfuls on purpose" for weak believers. Selwyn Hughes sees God dropping tokens of encouragement for his servants. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_215-23

**v. 17**
- Ruth worked from sunrise to sunset. An ephah was about 22 litres, a big day's earnings. Guzik draws lessons from it for studying God's word. EW

**v. 18**
- The leftover food was a blessing for Naomi. EW

**v. 19**
- Boaz saw Ruth's need and met it with food and comfort, which is why Naomi blesses whoever noticed her. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_219-23

**v. 20**
- *Goel* means kinsman-redeemer. He could buy back family land, and in other cases avenge a death. Clarke and Barnes, at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/2-20.html
- Henry: Naomi suddenly remembers Boaz and sees the likeliest man in Bethlehem to set them up. Henry calls Christ "our Goel." Same page.
- Melvill (Biblical Illustrator) treats the *goel* at length as a picture of Christ, who must be our kinsman to redeem us. Same page.
- MacArthur: the *goel* "came to the rescue," and every kinsman-redeemer pictured Christ. Boaz had both the family tie and the means. https://gty.org/library/blog/B170216
- Naomi, who called herself "Mara" (bitter), now sees God working things for good. EW
- *Where they really differ:* is it God or Boaz "who has not withdrawn his kindness"?
  - **God:** Piper (desiringgod) says it is the LORD's kindness, since Boaz had only just begun to be kind to the dead; precept austin agrees with him. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-under-the-wings-of-god and https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_219-23
  - **God:** Keil explains God's kindness to the dead as his care for their widows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/2-20.htm
  - **Boaz:** A Gospel Coalition sermon says "fairly certainly" Boaz, while noting the NKJV suggests God. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/ruth-part-2-en/
  - **Boaz:** Pulpit leans the same way, because Boaz's kindness to the living *was* his kindness to the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/2-20.htm
  - **Unclear:** Benson and the Geneva notes read it as kindness once shown to the husband and sons, now continued to their widows. Same page.
- *Catholic translations also differ.* The Douay-Rheims gives the kindness to Boaz, who "hath kept [it] also to the dead." The NAB gives it to the LORD. https://biblehub.com/catholic/ruth/2-20.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees in "the dead" a hint of belief in life after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/2-20.html

**v. 21**
- Naomi's reaction amounts to "stay with Boaz," since he is both generous and a near kinsman. EW

**v. 22**
- Henry: being seen in another field would look like scorning Boaz's kindness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/2-20.html

**v. 23**
- Ruth followed Naomi's advice and stayed in Boaz's fields until the harvest ended. https://gty.org/library/blog/B170216
